question.knowledge_point: Computing the Acceleration of a Particle at a Given Moment Given Its Velocity Vector
question.problem:
The velocity vector $v=⟨u,v⟩,$ measured in $\text{m}/\text{s},$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
v=⟨{2}^{t-1},\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}⟩.
$$

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=1.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t-1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1})⟩ \\  & =⟨{2}^{t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(1) & =⟨{2}^{1-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2(1)}{({1}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨{2}^{0}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the magnitude of the acceleration, we compute $|a(1)|:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|a(1)| & =|⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{1}{2}⟩| \\  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{ln}^{2}⁡2+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4{ln}^{2}⁡2+1}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4{ln}^{2}⁡2+1}}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

judgment.reasoning: All 16 final answers agree with the mathematics and their own captured worked solutions. Two worked solutions contain intermediate errors that do not change their final answers: q-118755 drops the factor 1/2 from the negative-endpoint logarithmic limit; q-51075 incorrectly labels its discussion of statement III as 'Statement II is true.' Mathematical verification: q-2389 substitutes u=x^3+7 and integrates u^(-1/2); q-72566 integrates the denominator's logarithmic derivative; q-4463 rationalizes to 1/(sqrt(x+4)+2), giving 1/4. q-7156 differentiates velocity to (5,4t). q-121920 gives acceleration (ln 2,-1/2) at t=1, whose norm is sqrt(4(ln 2)^2+1)/2. q-121917 gives acceleration (4,2) at pi/8, whose norm is 2sqrt(5). q-7165 and q-121926 differentiate position twice, giving (4t^3,6) and (2,4e^(2t+5)); q-121932 gives (-4,-18) at t=1. q-74403 reduces the integrand to 3cos(2x)+1. q-49605 substitutes u=ln x to obtain 8 times the integral of u from 2 to 4, which is 48. q-73659 substitutes u=log_7(4x), with dx/x=(ln 7)du. q-69893 has semiaxes 2 and 5, so its denominators are 4 and 25. q-118755 has divergent half-line integrals tending to -infinity and +infinity; its ordinary whole-line improper integral therefore diverges, despite a zero symmetric principal value. q-51075 has two half-line integrals diverging to +infinity. Thus both statement questions have only II and III true. q-118774 has antiderivative -e^(-x^2), with convergent half-line integrals -1 and 1, totaling 0.
